Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-12
Start: 16:28 UTC
Duration: ~75m
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Lukas Nguyen (Redwood SRE); Mark Danvers (Nimbus ML), Sara Cho (Nimbus Infra), Dev Patel (Nimbus CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Deep dive on low-level GPU execution paths, kernel selection heuristics, and when TensorRT-LLM (TRTLLM) picks different kernels compared to vLLM-like runtimes.
- Investigated intermittent CUDA Graph instability observed on Nimbus staging with persistent KV enabled; likely related to eviction + graph capture interplay.
- Discussed batching strategies, quantization impacts, and on-prem PCIe/NVLink topology constraints for VPC/private deployment.
- Agreed on concrete next steps: run paired benchmarks, collect kernel traces, and repro CUDAGraph edge case with controlled eviction.

Topics: kernel selection, CUDAGraph capture vs replay, KV cache eviction, continuous batching, quantization (4-bit/8-bit), NUMA/NVLink topology, on-prem mount points, regression detection.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
00:00 Alex: hey hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about 75 mins on the calendar so we can go deep. quick intro — alex from redwood ae, priya se on the runtime side, lukas on infra. mark sara dev from nimbus?
00:07 Mark: yeah thanks alex. we run a mixed workload: chat sessions and high-throughput embedding generation. recently saw some spikes when we enabled persistent KV cache and turned on CUDA Graph for steady-state.
00:15 Priya: got it. can you describe the spike pattern? is it latency tail or complete instability?
00:20 Mark: mostly tail, sometimes a few requests hang for a few seconds, and occasionally the whole worker evicts and we see fallback restarts. logs show cudagraph errors but it's messy.
00:30 Lukas: i also noticed memory fragmentation, plus on our racks NVLink meshes are not uniform — some boxes have full NVLink pairs, others are cross-chassis. could that matter?
00:38 Priya: yeah topology definitely changes peer-to-peer perf and affects kernel choice if the runtime detects different bandwidth. also cudagraph capture captures a specific mem layout; if the KV cache eviction changes pointers during replay you can hit invalid accesses or non-deterministic behavior.
00:47 Dev: hmm. we thought cudagraph was stable once captured. are you saying eviction can change pointer locations and break a captured graph?
00:52 Priya: exactly. when we capture a graph we expect the input buffers and their device addresses to be stable. persistent KV does pointer-churn — evict/prefetch moves tensors around if the memory manager compacts or migrates. that mismatch between capture-time addresses and replay-time addresses is a classic gotcha.
01:05 Alex: to add, some kernels used by TRTLLM bind to tensors in-place and don't re-resolve addresses on replay. vLLM path tends to rebuild certain exec paths more often which is safer but higher overhead. so there's a tradeoff: more aggressive cudagraph usage for perf vs robustness with dynamic replay.
01:18 Mark: okay that matches. we also saw differences when testing TRTLLM-quant 4-bit vs vLLM-int8 quant workflows; the latency distributions flip flop. any ideas why quantization changes kernel selection so much?
01:26 Priya: two reasons: first, quant kernels have different memory layout and alignment constraints, that can nudge the kernel selection heuristics. second, after quantization the compute-bound vs memory-bound balance changes — you might prefer different GEMM kernels or fused attention paths. TRT tends to choose very specialized int8/4bit kernels which are faster but more brittle to shape/pad changes.
01:39 Sara: so should we avoid 4-bit in production? we need cost savings but not at the expense of SLO misses.
01:44 Priya: it's workload dependent. we recommend running a sample of real traffic; for short sequence chat, 4-bit can be great. for variable long sequences with heavy KV interactions, 8-bit or q4_0 variants with some fallback make sense. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profile per route.
01:59 Dev: and what about batching? we run continuous batching with a 10ms window; will that interact with cudagraph or KV in weird ways?
02:05 Lukas: our infra batches at the GPU driver stage sometimes which can increase address reuse and make cudagraph more stable, but it also increases prefix pad variability which may change kernel selection.
02:12 Priya: yes — batching helps throughput but inflates max latency for first token; kernel selectors often look at token length distribution. if your batching mixes short and long, you may trigger different attention kernel variants. also eviction frequency increases if batching raises memory pressure.
02:25 Mark: any tuning knobs you suggest? we are on-prem (VPC-like) with mixed NVLink config.
02:29 Priya: a few: 1) prefer stable memory addresses during capture — pin persistent KV allocations and avoid compaction during steady-state. 2) limit autoscales that reallocate large pools during capture windows. 3) if using cuda graphs, capture at a representative batch/seq configuration and plan capture refresh on config change. 4) tune your batch micro-window (e.g., 5-12ms) and cap max batch size to avoid kernel path flips.
02:49 Alex: also, for TRTLLM we can control kernel heuristics — there's a fallback policy we use: in our infra you can force-safe-mode where we bias to replayable kernels, or aggressive-mode that picks fastest kernels even if they assume pinned addresses. we expose that as a config in Dedicated/Private deployments.
03:01 Sara: is that the same as disabling cudagraph?
03:03 Priya: related but different. disabling cudagraph forces dynamic kernel launches every step which is slower; safe-mode still uses graphs but with constraints (like pinned allocs, non-movable buffers). disabling is blunt.
03:12 Mark: how do we diagnose which kernel was chosen? we tried nvidia-smi but that's coarse.
03:16 Priya: we provide kernel traces — lightweight hooks that log kernel name, grid/block dims, shared mem usage, and the path (TRTLLM exec node id vs vLLM op). priya: (laughs) the traces aren't pretty but they help correlate tail events with kernel mismatches.
03:30 Lukas: we'll need those traces. our SREs are worried about log size. can you compress or sample?
03:33 Priya: yes we sample and compress; we can also do a focused trace capture for the 5min repro window. we'll attach a dek (sic) — link to spreadsheet and trace bucket: https://redwood.ai/internal/perf-spreadsheet (placeholder).
03:45 Dev: back to eviction: you mentioned pointer churn. could NUMA migrations cause similar issues? our VMs sometimes get memory migrated across NUMA nodes under load.
03:52 Priya: absolutely. NUMA migration changes physical locality; if that triggers GPU direct RDMA or host staging changes, the device addresses could be different. On-prem setups with non-uniform NVLink can add another layer. The runtime attempts to detect address stability but it's not perfect.
04:08 Mark: so for reproducible cudagraphs we need stable topology, pinned device allocations, and controlled eviction frequency. any way to avoid eviction entirely?
04:15 Lukas: persistent KV size a bit bigger so we avoid eviction is one path, plus intelligently purging cold keys to keep churn low. Redwood Optimize suggested an eviction threshold; can you recommend numbers?
04:24 Priya: we typically set persistent KV to 1.2x working set for steady sort workloads. if your working set is 12GB, set PVK to ~15GB to allow small churn. also tune prefetch to be async and non-blocking.
04:36 Alex: note also that for TRTLLM, using quantized weights in GPU memory vs host-mapped pages changes eviction semantics — GPU resident quant tensors are cheaper to keep pinned.
04:46 Mark: we also ran a test where TRTLLM had lower P99 on short sequences but vLLM was more stable under high concurrency. what explains that?
04:54 Priya: TRTLLM is optimized for low-latency kernel fusions and aggressive scheduling; it wins for tightly shaped, stable inputs. vLLM's more dynamic operator-level execution rebuilds kernels and tolerates shape variability — so it trades some speed for robustness. under high concurrency, the dynamic scheduler avoids catastrophic graph mismatches.
05:13 Dev: are there hybrid options? pick TRT for hot routes and vLLM for cold ones?
05:17 Alex: yes — Redwood’s smart routing can route by route or by load: hot paths go to TRTLLM dedicated pools, fall back to vLLM pools on errors or high-eviction rates. We can set a canary and rollout policy.
05:28 Sara: for on-prem we want the same flexibility. how invasive is switching runtime? do we need to reload models?
05:32 Priya: model artifacts are same; the runtime variant controls kernels and quant profiles. you can hot-swap endpoints but need to pin model version and ensure compatible KV formats. we recommend a canary with traffic split 90/10 then ramp.
05:45 Mark: what about automating detection of cudagraph brittleness? can Redwood alert on replay failures?
05:50 Alex: yes, Console includes alerts on replay mismatch, kernel launch failures, and eviction-induced fallbacks. We also have a perf-regression detector that compares recent traces to baseline and flags kernel-path shifts.
05:59 Priya: one more operational note: when capturing graphs in a private cluster, avoid background defrag or frequent CUDA context resets (some orchestration platforms do this). consider isolating GPU nodes for capture windows.
06:12 Dev: good call. ok concrete plan?
06:15 Alex: summarize next steps — Redwood runs paired benchmarks, we capture traces, share spreadsheet, and then joint repro session. agreed?
06:22 Mark: yes. also we'll try the safe-mode config on one node and run smoke tests.
06:27 Sara: SRE will send us NVLink topology and host memory layout by EOD.
06:31 Alex: perfect. we'll create ticket ff-1628 and attach artifacts.
